title: John Hammond's role in mixing studio bands and the Goodman Trio
summary: Wilson credits Hammond with pressing Goodman to hire him publicly and with breaking the color line among radio staff musicians.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: But there must have been somebody or someone that had seen -- well, you are the one who can do this, you are the one that can pull this off.

Well, the credit for that thing is -- and we're jumping a little bit ahead of our story, but this is very important and we can go back to the story. -- John Hammond has to have all the credit for that because he was the driving force behind the scenes of forming that Goodman Trio and putting me on an equal basis with Krupa in public -- away from the recording studio. But in public, right out in the open, he pushed and pressured Goodman to add me on as a regular member of the band, because Goodman and I had made many records in the studio; the Goodman Trio was born in the studio as far back as 1934, before Goodman was ever a bandleader, you know?

And I had played on records organized by Red Norvo; I made a lot of records with Krupa, with little groups^ Jack Teagarden and Charlie Teagarden and you probably did, too, all the mixed bands in those days did.
Eddie Lang, Even back in the twenties, used to record with Lonnie Johnson and all those great jazz groups*-- they were racially mixed in those days.
(Ed. note- Lang recorded with Johnson in 1928-29 as "Blind Willie Dunn".)
As a matter of fact, the Chocolate Dandies under Benny Carter -- two of the Chocolate Dandies were white when I did it -- Max Kaminsky and Floyd O'Brien were two of the white Chocolate Dandies.
But that was in the studio, now.
Yeah, he was tremendous; he did so much for that.

See, he could do that -- he had enough power and know how. He was a very smart man, you know, and jumping forward a little bit, when the color line was broken with the staff radio musicians, you know, John Hammond called on the phone the President of the corporation and said to mix up the band and that he wanted a mixed band in the studio, so they did it. And the NAACP was having rallies in Madison Square Garden and marching up and down the street, and nothing was happening. Here John Hammond gets on the phone, and breaks the color line in studio musicians -- Specs Powell, and I think you were there, and Cozy Cole, right.

And he did the same thing in 1936 with the Goodman Trio. And Goodman went along with it, you know, and a lot of those people at MCA were telling Goodman, you're a young man coming up and you're a great clarinet player and you start this racial mix and you're gonna stop

your career before you ever get started.
But it just so happened it was the other way around. Hammond was right. Goodman became one of the most successful musicians financially in the business because of the race thing. The tremendous spotlight of pioneering. And then after that, everybody began mixing -- Billie Holiday joined Artie Shaw's band and Charlie Shavers joined Tommy Dorsey.
